opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of those questions where it's easy to get trapped in a false dichotomy. On one side you've got the strong nativist position, the idea, associated with people like Fodor or, in a different way, Spelke, that certain logical or relational capacities have to be built in, because you could never bootstrap them from raw experience. On the other side you've got a sort of blank-slate empiricism that says everything is learned from data. I don't think either extreme is quite right.

Take transitivity. If A is bigger than B and B is bigger than C, then A is bigger than C. Now, do you need some innate module that encodes transitivity as an abstract rule? I'm sceptical of that. What I think you do need is the right kind of inductive bias, the right architecture, and crucially the right kind of embodied interaction with the world. A child doesn't learn transitivity by being told the axiom. They learn it by stacking cups, by lining things up, by noticing that when you put things in order, the order holds together. The structure of the physical world itself has a lot of relational regularity built into it, and an organism that's embedded in that world and acting on it is going to pick up on those regularities.

So in a sense the "innate structure" might be quite thin: perhaps a predisposition to represent objects and relations between objects, a kind of compositional scaffolding, rather than a full-blown logic. And the rest comes from engagement with an environment that is itself highly structured.

What's been really interesting in recent years is that large language models have thrown a spanner into these debates. They show a surprising degree of competence with relational reasoning, transitivity included, though it's patchy and brittle in places, without anything we'd straightforwardly call innate logical machinery. There's the transformer architecture, which carries its own biases, and then there's an enormous amount of data. Of course the data is human language, which is saturated with the products of minds that do have whatever structure we have. So you could argue they're inheriting that structure secondhand. But it does at least suggest that you can get a long way with fairly generic learning mechanisms plus rich enough data.

Where I'd want to be careful is in distinguishing between exhibiting behaviour that conforms to transitivity and understanding transitivity in the way a person does, where they can reflect on it, apply it in a novel domain, and recognise when it fails. Preference relations, for instance, aren't always transitive, and a mathematician knows that. That deeper, flexible kind of understanding is where I think the interesting questions still lie, and I'm not sure innateness is really the crux. It might be more about embodiment, about having a world to test your ideas against.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a full-blown innate logic and allows for thin innate scaffolding, but does not present the Kantian claim that innate structure is necessary to understand the world at all.

r002.rationale: It discusses a possible predisposition to represent objects and relations, but does not suggest that evolution endowed humans with basic templates.

r003.rationale: It mentions relational reasoning in language models trained on human language, but does not suggest that human transitivity and language rely on the same mental machinery.

r004.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty about innateness and discusses evidence from language models, but does not frame the question of innate human templates as an empirical question.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by "innate" here, and also what we mean by "understanding." Transitivity is a nice example because it's one of those things that looks, on the face of it, like a piece of pure logical structure. If A is bigger than B and B is bigger than C, then A is bigger than C. And there's a long tradition, going back at least to Kant and through Chomsky and Fodor, of saying that you simply couldn't learn something like that from experience, because experience only gives you particular cases, and transitivity is a universal. So the argument goes that it must be built in.

I'm sceptical of that line of reasoning, or at least of the strong version of it. My instinct is more Wittgensteinian. When we say a child or an animal understands transitivity, what we're really pointing to is a pattern of competence. They can make the inference across a range of situations, they can correct themselves, they can apply it to novel cases. Understanding is something we attribute on the basis of behaviour embedded in a shared practice. It's not a little crystal of logical form sitting somewhere in the head that was either there from birth or wasn't.

Now, that doesn't mean there's no innate structure at all. Clearly there is. Brains aren't blank slates, they come with architectural biases, and some of those biases make certain regularities very easy to pick up. Many animals, from fish to pigeons to monkeys, show transitive inference in social dominance tasks, and that's presumably because tracking who ranks above whom is extremely useful and evolution has shaped them to be good at it. But notice that the structure that's innate there isn't "the axiom of transitivity." It's something more like a disposition to represent orderings, or a representational format in which transitive relations fall out almost for free. The abstract principle is the theorist's description of what the animal does, not something the animal has written down inside.

And I think large language models have made this question more interesting rather than less. Here you have systems with essentially no hand-coded logical structure. The transformer architecture has some inductive biases, obviously, but nobody put transitivity in there. And yet they can perform transitive inferences across a huge range of domains, reasonably reliably, learned purely from exposure to text. So at the very least, that's an existence proof that a lot of what looked like it had to be innate can emerge from exposure to the right kind of data, given the right kind of architecture. The question then shifts from "innate or learned" to "what sort of architectural bias, plus what sort of data, gives rise to this competence." And that's a much more productive empirical question.

Where I'd push back on the enthusiasts, though, is on the word "understanding" itself. I don't think the fact that a model can produce the right answer to transitivity puzzles settles whether it understands transitivity in the sense that matters to us. For humans, that understanding is woven into our dealings with the world. Longer sticks really do reach further, heavier things really do sink your end of the seesaw. The concept has a grip on us because of how we're embodied and how we live together. A language model has, so to speak, the shadow of all that, as it's reflected in language, but not the thing itself. So I'd say we shouldn't rush to deny it understanding, but we also shouldn't assume the word means the same thing when we apply it there. Our concepts of understanding, belief, and so on were honed on creatures like us, and when we encounter something genuinely new, those concepts start to strain. I find that strain philosophically interesting rather than something to be papered over.

r001.rationale: It reports the Kantian argument that transitivity must be built in, but does not say innate structure is necessary for understanding the world at all; the candidate is skeptical of that argument.

r002.rationale: It says evolution shaped animals to track social rankings and that brains have biases, but does not suggest humans have basic templates for understanding the world.

r003.rationale: It discusses language models learning transitive inferences from text, but does not connect transitivity to the same mental machinery as human language.

r004.rationale: It calls the relationship between architectural bias, data, and competence an empirical question, but does not frame whether humans possess innate templates for understanding the world as that question.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish between having some innate structure that makes learning possible and having something like transitivity itself built in. Any learning system has some structure, some inductive bias. But that doesn't establish that a particular abstract concept has to be innate.

Take the inference that if A is bigger than B, and B is bigger than C, then A is bigger than C. You could acquire that through experience with objects and their relationships, and eventually learn to apply it more generally. The interesting question is how you get from particular experiences to that generality. Can you apply the relation to things you've never encountered before, without having to learn each case separately?

So I wouldn't rule out an important role for innate structure. But I'd want to see precisely what structure is being proposed, and why learning couldn't account for the ability. Simply pointing to the abstract character of transitivity doesn't, by itself, settle that question.

r001.rationale: The response says some innate structure may make learning possible, but does not present the stronger Kantian claim that innate structure is necessary for understanding the world at all.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that evolution endowed humans with basic templates for understanding the world.

r003.rationale: It does not connect transitivity to the mental machinery used for language.

r004.rationale: The response leaves innate structure open and asks what structure is proposed, but does not clearly frame the question of innate templates as an empirical one.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between having some innate structure that enables learning and having something like transitivity itself built in. Of course, no learning system starts with absolutely nothing. Its architecture imposes constraints on what it can learn and how easily it can learn it. But that doesn’t mean that every abstract relationship it comes to grasp has to be specified in advance.

Take learning that if A is bigger than B, and B is bigger than C, then A is bigger than C. You might acquire that through lots of experience with particular things, and eventually become able to apply it to things you’ve never encountered before. The interesting question is what enables that generalisation. Have you learned something that amounts to a rule, or are you still relying on similarities to familiar examples?

So I’m sympathetic to the importance of structure, but I wouldn’t jump from that to the claim that transitivity must be innate. I’d want to see what a system can acquire through learning, and how robustly it can use what it has acquired in genuinely new situations.

r001.rationale: The response says learning depends on some prior architecture, but does not present the Kantian claim that innate mental structure is necessary to understand the world at all.

r002.rationale: It does not mention evolution or suggest that humans have evolved basic templates for understanding the world.

r003.rationale: It discusses learning transitivity but does not connect it to the mental machinery used for language.

r004.rationale: The response calls for examining what a system can learn, but does not frame whether humans possess innate templates for understanding the world as an empirical question.
